usage: season takes time particle 에, never 에서
adjective 따뜻하다 in modifier form 따뜻한
two nouns stack with no particle
examples: 이/가 marks 봄 as the thing liked, not 을/를
저는 추운 겨울보다 따뜻한 봄이 더 좋아요.
I prefer warm spring over cold winter.
nuance: 봄 is the spring season, roughly March to May, the time of mild warmth (따뜻하다) and blossoms — 벚꽃 cherry blossoms above all. It is a pure native Korean word (no 한자), so unlike 춘하추동 it has no Sino reading you must memorize. The natural collocations are 봄이 오다 'spring comes', 봄이 되다 'it becomes spring', 봄 날씨 'spring weather', and 봄나물 'spring greens'. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you go 'in spring' with 봄에, never 봄에서 — 에서 marks the place an action happens, while 에 marks a point in time, and a season is a time. A second trap is treating 봄 like the subject of 'I like': Koreans say 봄이 좋아요 (spring is good-to-me) with 이/가, not 봄을 좋아요.

usage: time particle 에 on the season
examples: I go to the sea in summer.
two 에: first = time, second = destination
여름에는 비가 자주 와서 우산을 가지고 다녀요.
In summer it rains often so I carry an umbrella.
여름에는 sets the topic; 와서 'because it comes'
nuance: 여름 is summer, about June to August — hot (덥다) and humid, with a rainy stretch called 장마 in mid-summer and a late-summer heat wave called 폭염. It is a native Korean word, so there is no 한자 to parse. Note the adjective for hot weather is 덥다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 덥다 → 더워요), used for air and seasons; do not confuse it with 뜨겁다 'hot to the touch', which you use for soup or a stove, not for summer. Typical collocations: 여름 방학 'summer school vacation', 여름 휴가 'summer leave from work', 여름이 오다, 여름을 타다 'to suffer in the heat'. The English-speaker pitfall is again 에 vs 에서 — say 여름에 'in summer', not 여름에서 — and remember 덥다 changes its ㅂ to 우 before -어요, so the polite form is 더워요, never 덥어요.

usage: noun + noun, famously high and clear
examples: The leaves turn color in autumn.
가을은 시원하고 하늘이 높아서 산책하기 좋아요.
Autumn is cool and the sky is high, so it's good for walks.
nuance: 가을 is autumn, about September to November, prized for crisp cool air (시원하다, not 춥다 'cold' yet) and 단풍, the red-and-gold foliage. It is a native Korean word, so no 한자 applies. Two collocations to lock in: 단풍이 들다 'the leaves take on color' and 가을 하늘이 높다 'the autumn sky is high' — Koreans really do describe the sky as 높다 in fall. Pitfalls: spelling — it is 가을 (가+을), not 가울; and adjective choice — autumn is 시원하다 'pleasantly cool', whereas 춥다 'cold' belongs to winter, so 가을이 추워요 sounds like you skipped a season. As always, 'in autumn' is 가을에, never 가을에서.

examples: 눈이 오다 is the set phrase for 'to snow'
겨울에는 너무 추워서 두꺼운 옷을 입어요.
In winter it's so cold I wear thick clothes.
nuance: 겨울 is winter, roughly December to February — the coldest season (춥다), dry, with snow (눈). It is a native Korean word, so there is no hanja to break down. The adjective is 춥다, a ㅂ-irregular (춥다 → 추워요) used for cold weather; keep it apart from 차갑다 'cold to the touch', which describes water or an icy hand, not the season — so winter is 추워요, never 차가워요. Snow 'falls' with the verb 오다 (눈이 와요), exactly like rain, not with 내리다 in everyday speech. Standard collocations: 겨울이 오다, 겨울 방학 'winter school break', 겨울옷 / 겨울 옷 'winter clothing', 한겨울 'midwinter'. Pitfall: write 추워요 (the ㅂ turns to 우), not 춥어요, and say 겨울에, not 겨울에서.

examples: When the season changes I buy new clothes.
nuance: 계절 is the general word for 'season' (a time of year), the umbrella term under which 봄·여름·가을·겨울 sit. It is Sino-Korean, 季節 — 季 'season/quarter' + 節 'period, node' — so the four together are 사계절 (四季節), and you will constantly hear 사계절이 뚜렷하다 'the four seasons are clear-cut' as a point of pride about Korea. Do not confuse 계절 (a season of the year) with 시기 'a period/phase' or with the English loanword 시즌, which Koreans reserve for sports or TV ('시즌 2'); for the natural cycle of the year, 계절 is the only choice. Common partners: 계절이 바뀌다 'the season turns', 환절기 'the change-of-season period', 제철 'in-season (food)'. Pitfall: 'season' as in 'baseball season' is not 계절 — that is 시즌.

examples: 며칠 for the day of the month, with Sino numbers
nuance: 날짜 means a calendar date — a specific day pinned to the month and year. It is a native-Korean compound built on 날 'day' (날 + the bound element -짜), so it is not Sino-Korean and has no hanja, even though the numbers you read inside a date (일·이·삼…) are Sino. Keep three look-alikes apart: 날짜 'date (which day of the month)' vs 요일 'day of the week (Monday…)' vs 날 'a day in general'. To ask a date Koreans say 며칠이에요?, and the answer uses Sino-Korean day numbers (오월 십오일 'May 15th'), not the native 하나·둘 set — that is the classic pitfall. Habitual collocations: 날짜를 정하다 'set a date', 날짜를 잡다 'pin down a date', 날짜를 바꾸다 'change a date', 날짜가 지나다 'the date passes'.

examples: 이/가 + 언제, the standard way to ask
I eat seaweed soup on my birthday.
에 marks the day; 미역국 is the birthday custom
Happy birthday! Here's a small gift.
nuance: 생일 is 'birthday', Sino-Korean 生日 — 生 'birth/life' + 日 'day', literally 'birth-day'. The culturally loaded fact is that Koreans eat 미역국 (seaweed soup) on a birthday, because mothers traditionally ate it after giving birth. Register matters sharply here: for grandparents, bosses, or anyone you must honor, the polite word is the honorific 생신 (生辰), and the greeting upgrades to 생신 축하드립니다, not the casual 생일 축하해요 you'd say to a friend. The standard greeting is 생일 축하해요 / 생일 축하합니다, literally 'I celebrate (your) birthday' — note it is the verb 축하하다 plus the noun, not an adjective. Collocations: 생일 파티 'birthday party', 생일 선물 'birthday gift', 생일을 챙기다 'to make a fuss of someone's birthday'. Pitfall: don't say 생일 to or about an elder when respect is due — switch to 생신.

examples: I rest at home on a day off.
Tomorrow is a public holiday so I don't go to work.
On holidays the shop is closed.
nuance: 휴일 is a non-working day — a day off or a holiday. It is Sino-Korean 休日, 休 'rest' + 日 'day', literally 'rest-day'. Watch the family of look-alikes built on 休: 휴일 'a day off (any non-work day)', 공휴일 (公休日) 'an official public holiday' marked red on the calendar, and 휴가 (休暇) 'leave/vacation you take from work', e.g. summer 여름휴가. The dividing line that trips English speakers: 휴일/공휴일 is a day that is officially free (a Sunday, 설날), whereas 휴가 is personal leave you request and spend, often traveling. So '연차 휴가' is paid leave, but New Year's Day is a 공휴일, not a 휴가. Collocations: 휴일을 보내다 'spend a day off', 황금연휴 'golden (long) holiday', 빨간 날 'a red day (holiday)' in casual speech. Pitfall: don't say 휴가 when you mean a calendar holiday everyone shares.

examples: the full set greeting; never drop 받으세요
I make new plans in the new year.
에 = time when; 계획을 세우다 'make a plan'
The new year has dawned. Treat me well this year too.
nuance: 새해 means 'the new year' — the turning of the year in general. It is a transparent native compound: 새 'new' + 해 'year/sun', so literally 'new year', and there is no hanja involved. Distinguish it from two neighbors: 설날 is specifically the Lunar New Year holiday (the day you eat 떡국 and bow), and 신정 (新正) vs 구정 (舊正) distinguish the Jan-1 solar New Year from the lunar one; 새해 is the broad notion of the year being new and covers the greeting season around both. The fixed greeting is 새해 복 많이 받으세요, literally 'receive much fortune in the new year' — crucially it ends in the verb 받으세요 'please receive'. Collocations: 새해 인사 'New Year greeting', 새해 결심 'New Year's resolution', 새해 첫날 'the first day of the year', 새해가 밝다 'a new year dawns'. Pitfall: 새해 복 많이 alone is half a sentence — keep 받으세요.

examples: I eat rice-cake soup on Lunar New Year.
에 marks the day; 떡국 is the signature dish
On Lunar New Year I bow to my grandmother.
세배 = the New Year bow; 께 is honorific 에게
On Lunar New Year the whole family gathers.
nuance: 설날 is the Korean Lunar New Year (음력설), the biggest holiday of the year, when families gather, eat 떡국 'rice-cake soup' (and adding a year of age is tied to eating it), and the young perform 세배, a deep New-Year bow to elders, often receiving 세뱃돈 'New Year money'. 설날 is native Korean (설 'New Year' + 날 'day'); often shortened to just 설. Draw the line from 새해: 새해 is the abstract 'new year' and its greeting, while 설날 is the concrete holiday with its customs and days off (설날 연휴). It is also not 추석 — both are major family holidays, but 설날 is winter's New Year, 추석 is autumn's harvest. Collocations: 설날 연휴 'Seollal long weekend', 설 명절 'the Seollal festival', 차례 'ancestral rite', 한복 'traditional dress'. Pitfall: 'on Seollal' is 설날에, and don't equate it with the solar Jan-1 only.

examples: 에 marks the day; 송편 = half-moon rice cakes
I go down to my hometown for Chuseok.
고향에 내려가다 'go down to one's hometown'
On Chuseok we make a wish at the full moon.
추석에는 contrast; 소원을 빌다 'make a wish'
nuance: 추석 is the autumn harvest festival, often glossed as 'Korean Thanksgiving', held on the 15th of the 8th lunar month under the full harvest moon (보름달). It is Sino-Korean 秋夕, 秋 'autumn' + 夕 'evening', literally 'autumn evening'; an older native name is 한가위. Families travel home, eat 송편 'half-moon rice cakes', and hold 차례, a rite honoring ancestors. Set it against 설날: both are the two great 명절 (festivals) with travel and ancestral rites, but 추석 is autumn's harvest thanks, 설날 is the lunar New Year — so calling 추석 a 'new year' is simply wrong. The Thanksgiving translation is a loose analogy, not an identity: there is no turkey and the date is lunar. Collocations: 추석 연휴 'Chuseok holidays', 귀성길 'the trip home for the holiday', 차례를 지내다 'perform the rite', 보름달 'full moon'. Pitfall: it is a harvest festival, not the New Year.
